name: Kira Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a drill operator at the Blackwater iron ore mine, and these days I lead the blast-hole drilling crew. Half my week I'm in the cab of a drill rig on the bench, drilling the holes the blasters fill, and the other half I'm in the operations room watching two drills that run on autopilot and stepping in when they get confused. I start at six, check the drill pattern on the tablet, ask an AI assistant to flag anything odd in last night's data, then go out. I like solving problems, and what wears me out is the pace when the pattern changes three times in one shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on the autopilot drills?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put my hand up. When they announced the trial three years ago most of the senior drillers said no thanks, and I thought, if it's coming anyway I'd rather be the one who knows how it works. My partner Jonas teaches maths at the high school, and he helped me with the coding course at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they're not magic, which is what I already tell people. I use AI every day for small stuff and it's handy, but it never ran a bench. I'd probably post something a bit cheeky about all the people who said we'd be gone by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a little disappointed. I've bet a fair bit of my career on this stuff being important. If it stalls, I'm a good driller with a few extra skills, which is still a decent place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing both roles and keep learning, because the tools still save time. I'd probably push the company to use the savings to fix the roster rather than cut people. Money stays the same, we keep saving our usual 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small pinch of disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said disappointed. What were you hoping AI would do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the boring, dangerous bits off us. Standing on a bench in forty-degree heat changing drill bits isn't noble, it's just hard. I wanted the machines to take that while we did the thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the senior drillers who said no say to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd rib me for a month, no doubt. Marcus would leave a tin-foil hat on my seat. I'd laugh, he'd laugh, and we'd get on with it.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are useful but not magic, which is what I already tell people. I'd probably post something cheeky about everyone who said we'd be gone by now.
S0.think: Honestly I'd be a little disappointed, because I've bet a fair bit of my career on this. If it stalls I'm still a good driller with extra skills, which is a decent place to be.
S0.do: Keeps working both the cab and the operations room and keeps learning the tools. Pushes the company to spend the time savings on a better roster, and keeps saving the usual 300 a month.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small pinch of disappointment.
S0.quote: Standing on a bench in forty-degree heat changing drill bits isn't noble, it's just hard.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is the rare worker who'd be let down if AI stalls, because she wanted it to take the dangerous work. She still frames the gains as something workers should share. She is relaxed and teasing about colleagues who were sceptical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when the union needs to get ahead of it. I'd say it's not the robots that decide who gets hurt, it's the deal. I'd be pushing for every driller to get paid training and a guaranteed spot if they want one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. I already run the autopilot drills, so I'm the person they'd need. What bothers me is that being in a good spot while my crew isn't feels rotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd offer to train the rest of the crew on the autopilot system, on paid time. I'd ask the union delegate to make that part of the next agreement. I'd also take the next level of the remote operations course, about six weeks of night study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, uneasy for the crew. I'd feel a bit guilty, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hendrik. He's 61, drills by feel, hears a bit going before the sensor does. He's never sent a text in his life. I'd want him to finish on full pay doing something useful, maybe mentoring, not shoved out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a promotion that meant fewer drillers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about this. I'd take it if the deal for the others was decent, because someone who cares should be in that chair. If they're just using me to cut the crew, no.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this now, because it's the deal, not the robots, that decides who gets hurt. I'd push for every driller to get paid training and a guaranteed spot.
S1.think: Privately I'm in a good spot because I already run the autopilot drills. Being safe while my crew isn't would feel rotten, though.
S1.do: Offers to train the rest of the crew on the autopilot system on paid time and asks the union delegate to write it into the next agreement. Takes the next six-week remote operations course at night.
S1.feel: Calm for herself and uneasy for her crew, with some guilt.
S1.quote: Being in a good spot while my crew isn't feels rotten.
S1.fieldNote: Kira is personally secure here and knows it, and her worry is guilt about her crew. She'd only take a promotion that cuts drillers if the deal for them is fair. She puts her skills to use for others through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, fast: a tax on the companies using it and a basic income while people work out what's next. I'd say it online and at every meeting. I'd say the people who own the robots shouldn't keep all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it rattles me more than I'd admit. If AI can run the drills and fix them, my operations job goes too, maybe a year after the drillers. Being early only buys me a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd look hard at the money: we have about four months saved, so I'd push that toward six and stop the overseas holiday we'd booked. I'd try to get on the team that sets up the new systems, because someone has to install them, even briefly. And I'd throw myself into the campaign for a public share of the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel I can steer, but the road's narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what does being early actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year of work after the others, and a better payout. That's real money for a family. But two years is too short to build anything new, so I'd be riding the wave out, not surfing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his job is probably safer than mine for a while, kids still need a person in the room. And I'd ask him if we should sell the boat. He'd say yes before I finished the sentence.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency rules fast, with a tax on companies using it and a basic income while people adjust. The people who own the robots shouldn't keep all of it.
S2.think: It rattles me more than I'd admit, because if AI can run and fix the drills my operations job goes too. Being early only buys me a little.
S2.do: Pushes savings from four toward six months, cancels an overseas holiday and talks about selling the boat. Tries to join the team installing the new systems and campaigns for a public share of the profits.
S2.feel: Anxious but still feeling able to steer.
S2.quote: Two years is too short to build anything new, so I'd be riding the wave out, not surfing it.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most prepared driller I've met admits two years outruns her. Her response is practical: get on the install team, trim the household, and campaign for a public share. Her partner's teaching job is the family's anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say we've got time to make it fair if we start right now. I'd be pushing the union to set up a transition fund straight away, before the mine sees the savings. And I'd be telling the young ones to learn the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to build a second career that uses what I know. Maybe training others on autonomous systems across different mines, or working for a public body checking these systems are safe. My job goes, but I'd be standing somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a short course in safety auditing for automated equipment, and I'd ask the mine for a role writing their training material. We'd overpay the mortgage a bit and get savings to six months. I'd keep helping my crew through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a buzz, too, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choice. With two I'm grabbing what's left, with five I get to pick a direction. Three years is long enough to get a qualification and a reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel a buzz. Is that odd, given what's happening to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is, and I notice it. I can be excited about my own next step and angry about how it's being done to others. Both are true at once.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives us time to make it fair if we start now. I'd push the union for a transition fund before the mine sees the savings, and tell the young ones to learn the systems.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build a second career from what I know, maybe training or safety auditing for autonomous systems. My job goes, but I'd be standing somewhere.
S3.do: Starts a short safety auditing course for automated equipment in year one and asks to write the mine's training material. Overpays the mortgage, gets savings to six months and keeps supporting her crew through the union.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a guilty buzz of excitement.
S3.quote: I can be excited about my own next step and angry about how it's being done to others.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Kira moves from bracing to choosing, and she names the excitement she feels alongside her anger. She keeps both her own plan and her crew's in view. She pictures herself in a public safety role, which fits her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. Retraining for everyone, public money for it, and a say for workers on how it's rolled out. I'd want our mine to be the example other mines copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is plenty. I'd be 53 with a new career well underway. What I'd worry about is whether the country actually uses the time, because people tend to wait until the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the safety auditing qualification properly over two years, then move into it part time while still drilling. I'd help Jonas set up a robotics club at the school so our kids and their friends understand this stuff. We'd keep saving steadily and clear the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. My worry is for other people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the deal decides who gets hurt. Who decides the deal in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoever shows up. If workers sit back for nine years, the companies decide it. That's why I'd keep going to the boring meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira about her own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fourteen and wants to be a vet. I'd tell her go for it, and learn how the machines think while you're at it. I don't want her scared of it, I want her to know it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want public money for retraining, a worker say in rollout, and our mine as the example others copy.
S4.think: For me ten years is plenty, and I'd be 53 with a new career underway. My real worry is whether the country uses the time or waits until the last year.
S4.do: Takes a safety auditing qualification over two years, then moves into it part time while still drilling. Helps her partner start a robotics club at the school and clears the car loan while saving steadily.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with her worry aimed at other people.
S4.quote: Whoever shows up. If workers sit back for nine years, the companies decide it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Kira is calm for herself and turns her attention to whether society will use the time. She'd keep going to the dull meetings because she thinks presence decides outcomes. She wants her children to understand the technology rather than fear it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody gets to choose anything, they just get hit. What would help is a basic income set up in advance, so it's ready to switch on, and a law that gives workers a share of what automation saves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the bench at sunrise, honestly, the red dust lit up and the drill singing. I'd happily give up the heat, but not that.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the bench at sunrise, honestly, the red dust lit up and the drill singing.
portrait: Kira Farah is a 43-year-old blast-hole drilling lead at the Blackwater iron ore mine who volunteered for the autopilot drill trial and uses AI every day. Her partner teaches maths, and they have two kids and a mortgage. She'd be mildly disappointed if AI stalled, and in the steady picture she feels secure but guilty about her crew. Two years of warning makes her anxious because it outruns even her head start, while five or ten years lets her plan a move into training or safety auditing for automated equipment, always alongside union work for colleagues who can't follow.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because nobody would get to choose anything and people would just get hit.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income set up in advance and ready to switch on, and a law giving workers a share of what automation saves.
